title: Ethical legal and environmental impacts flash cards

cards.front: Which kind of issue concerns whether a decision is fair or morally responsible?
back: Ethical.

cards.front: Which kind of issue concerns whether an action meets the law?
back: Legal.

cards.front: Which kind of issue concerns waste, energy use or damage to habitats?
back: Environmental.

cards.front: What is personal data?
back: Information relating to an identifiable person.

cards.front: What is a wearable device?
back: A computing device worn on the body.

cards.front: What is cloud storage?
back: Storing data on remote servers accessed through a network.

cards.front: What does unauthorised access mean?
back: Access to a system without permission.

cards.front: Name one action that can reduce electronic waste.
back: Repair.

cards.front: Explain why legal conduct can still raise an ethical concern.
back: Law and ethics answer different questions: compliance with rules does not settle fairness.
For example, a workplace monitoring arrangement could meet legal requirements yet still create intrusive pressure on staff.

cards.front: A walking app stores every user's movements indefinitely. Explain a privacy risk.
back: Location history can reveal someone's home or routine.
Keeping a large identifiable record increases what could be exposed or misused if access is compromised.

cards.front: Explain data minimisation using a homework app.
back: Collect only information needed for the purpose.
For example, pupil identity and assignment submissions may be needed, while continuous location tracking is unnecessary.

cards.front: Explain one way mobile technology can improve access to services.
back: A person can use a phone while away from a fixed computer.
This lets them contact support, check directions or use a learning service wherever a suitable connection is available.

cards.front: Explain one reason cloud storage might interrupt a business's work.
back: Access depends on the provider and a working network connection.
An outage can prevent staff reaching the files needed for their tasks.

cards.front: Explain one security issue associated with an unsecured wireless network.
back: Traffic or access may be inadequately protected.
An attacker could intercept information or reach resources they should not be able to use.

cards.front: Explain why replacing an implant's software requires particular care.
back: The device may support an important bodily function.
A faulty update could interrupt that function, so reliable testing and safe maintenance matter.

cards.front: Explain one employment impact of autonomous vehicles.
back: Some driving roles could be reduced or changed.
Workers may need retraining, even if new maintenance or software jobs are created.

cards.front: Explain why a biometric health record is a privacy concern even if the company removes the user's name.
back: Other information may still allow the person to be identified.
Removing a name alone does not necessarily make sensitive data anonymous.

cards.front: Explain why an authorised security test differs from illegal hacking.
back: The tester has permission and works within an agreed scope.
Unauthorised access lacks that permission, even when the person claims a helpful intention.

cards.front: A company offers staff fitness trackers and plans to share individual activity data with managers. Explain an ethical concern and a safeguard.
back: Employees may feel pressured to participate because the employer has power over them.
Activity comparisons could unfairly disadvantage staff with different needs or circumstances.
A meaningful alternative and tightly limited access reduce pressure and unrelated use.

cards.front: Explain how repairable devices can reduce environmental harm.
back: Repair keeps useful equipment operating for longer.
This can reduce the need to mine materials and manufacture replacements.
It also reduces electronic waste, although running energy use still matters.

cards.front: A government argues that it needs access to private communications to prevent attacks. Explain its argument and a concern for citizens.
back: Access may help investigators identify threats or connections between suspects.
Broad monitoring also collects information about people who have done nothing wrong.
That information could be misused or exposed, reducing their privacy.

cards.front: Explain why a mobile-only public service could disadvantage some users.
back: Some users cannot afford a suitable device or data connection.
Others may have limited coverage or difficulty using the app.
They could be excluded from an essential service, so an accessible alternative is needed.

cards.front: Evaluate a school storing pupil work in the cloud.
back: Pupils and staff can access and share work from different locations.
Off-site storage may support recovery if local equipment is lost, when suitable backup arrangements exist.
Incorrect sharing permissions or compromised accounts can expose work and personal information.
It is useful if accounts, access and recovery arrangements are managed well; provider security alone does not protect a publicly shared folder.

cards.front: A smartwatch reports an unexpectedly high reading. Explain two risks of making decisions from unverified readings.
back: A reading may be inaccurate because of the sensor or how it is used.
Treating it as a diagnosis could create unnecessary worry or an inappropriate response.
An employer or insurer could use misleading data to make an unfair judgement about somebody.
The data needs appropriate verification and limits on its use; it is not a complete medical assessment.

cards.front: Explain environmental impacts at three stages in a phone's lifecycle and one way to reduce them.
back: **Manufacture:** mining materials can damage habitats; production uses energy.
**Use:** the phone and the services it accesses require electricity.
**Disposal:** unsuitable handling of electronic waste can release harmful substances.
Keeping the phone supported and repaired for longer can reduce replacement manufacture and waste.

cards.front: Explain why switching every meeting online does not automatically remove environmental harm.
back: Fewer journeys can reduce travel-related emissions.
However, computers and network equipment still require manufacture.
Running the devices, networks and data centres uses energy.
The net effect depends on the travel avoided and the equipment and electricity used.

cards.front: A connected medical implant sends identifiable readings to a clinic. Explain two benefits or risks of this connection.
back: Remote readings could help the clinic notice a problem without requiring every check in person.
This can improve convenience and support timely review.
Transmitted health information is sensitive and could be exposed by inadequate protection.
Secure access and reliable operation are needed because unauthorised control or an interrupted service may have serious consequences.

cards.front: Evaluate giving public Wi-Fi access in a town centre.
back: It may help residents and visitors reach information without using their own mobile data.
This improves access for some people, but still requires a suitable device.
Poorly protected connections or excessive tracking create security and privacy risks.
The service is more beneficial if access is inclusive, protection is suitable and unnecessary personal data is not collected.
